slides.title: What is measured and by which methods
bullets: Qualitative tests: protein, glucose, bilirubin, blood, ketone bodies, pH, urobilinogen, nitrites and specific gravity.
In primary-care laboratories reagent test strips that measure several components of urine are convenient and reliable.
As funds improve, a move from qualitative to semi-quantitative and full quantitative methods is recommended.
For semi-quantitative protein and glucose, test strips are preferable; for glucose the Benedict test also reacts with other sugars.
Boiling urine to detect protein is not recommended because it is hazardous; safer methods are chosen where possible.

slides.title: Using a test strip
bullets: 1. Take the strip out of its container and close the lid at once.
2. Mix uncentrifuged urine gently; dip one end of the strip into it and take it out at once.
3. Touch the edge of the strip to the container to remove excess liquid.
4. Compare the colour of the test zones with the colour scale on the container (the reading time is given in the strip instructions).
5. For pH an indicator paper can also be used: dip the strip, remove excess liquid and compare the colour with the scale on the package.
6. To save strips, each can be cut lengthwise in two with sharp scissors.

slides.title: Sulphosalicylic acid test for protein
bullets: 1. Put 5 mL of urine into a clean tube and mark it “N” (control).
2. Put 5 mL of urine into a second tube and mark it “T” (test).
3. Add 2 drops of 20% sulphosalicylic acid solution to the test tube with a dropper.
4. Compare the two tubes against a dark background: see whether turbidity has appeared in the test tube.
5. Grading: slight turbidity — +, moderate — ++, marked — +++, pronounced turbidity or precipitate — ++++.
6. In patients taking tolbutamide, penicillin, sulphonamides or para-aminosalicylic acid the result may be falsely positive.

slides.title: False results
bullets: Protein: false positives if disinfectants or vaginal or urethral discharge get into the sample, or if the urine is very alkaline.
Glucose: ascorbic acid and some drugs and high catalase activity give false negatives; residues of disinfectants such as bleaching powder give false positives.

Bilirubin: protect fresh urine from sunlight and fluorescent light — bilirubin oxidises quickly to biliverdin, for which the strip has no reagent; nitrites reduce sensitivity; phenazopyridine may give a false positive.
Positive results are pathological; if protein is found the urine is also examined microscopically.
If sugar is found in the urine of a patient not known to have diabetes, the blood is also tested.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: Industrially prepared solutions for checking the quality of test strips exist, but they are expensive.
Quality can be monitored by testing duplicates of specimens with standard biochemical methods in a larger laboratory and comparing the results.
Strips are stored in their closed container, which is closed again immediately after each use.

slides.title: Classic tests not covered here
bullets: The Aripova book does not recommend the boiling test for urine because it is dangerous, and advises giving up old ways of measuring pH such as methylene blue.

The classic tests in the Kurbonova textbook that use hot concentrated reagents, ammonia, nitroprusside or ferric chloride (Heller, Haynes, Lange, Garrison) are not included in this protocol — test strips are preferred; the classic tests need special reagents and precautions.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Specimen containers must have lids; the specimen must not spill out.
Wear single-use gloves when handling specimens; after work wash the hands with soap or wipe them with an alcohol solution.
Specimens are kept in a spill-proof container while being processed, stored and transported.

Pour leftover urine carefully, without splashing, into the toilet of the washing room; put containers and instruments into a disinfectant solution (concentration and time according to the regulation in force).
